# How to Build a Simple Customer FAQ for a Small Business with Copilot

> **In short:** Microsoft Copilot can draft a clean customer FAQ for your small business in about an hour — you give it your real questions and a few business facts, and it writes the answers. You'll still review and publish it yourself, because Copilot can't post to your website or send replies for you.

A customer FAQ (a list of Frequently Asked Questions) is one of the highest-leverage things a small business can write. Every time a customer emails the same question, or a new hire has to be told the same thing, a good FAQ quietly saves you an hour. The problem is that writing one from scratch feels overwhelming, especially if you've never done it. Copilot turns it into a conversation: you feed it your real questions, it drafts the answers, and you polish what it gives you. By the end of this guide you'll have a finished FAQ saved as a document you control.

## Before you start
- A free Microsoft account (the same one you might use for Outlook, OneDrive, or Xbox). If you don't have one, sign up at account.microsoft.com — it takes about two minutes.
- A device with a web browser, or the free Microsoft Copilot app on phone or desktop. No paid Copilot plan is required for this task.
- A rough list of 5–10 questions your customers actually ask. Pull them from recent emails, DMs, or your team's memory. Rough notes are fine.
- About 45–60 minutes total, with short breaks.

## Step 1 — Gather your real questions first
Before you open any AI tool, spend 10–15 minutes writing down the questions your customers truly ask. Open your email inbox, your Instagram DMs, your phone notes, or your support inbox and scan the last 30 days. Write down 5–10 questions that come up again and again. Don't try to make them sound polished — quick shorthand is enough. If you're brand new and don't have many messages yet, ask yourself what your team gets tired of explaining, or what new customers always seem confused about on day one.

💬 Example: a rough list might read "do you ship? / how long takes delivery? / can I return sale items? / do you do student discount? / where do I park?"

You'll know it worked when you have a short, honest list of real questions — not the polished ones you wish people asked, but the actual ones you keep answering.

## Step 2 — Open Copilot
Open your web browser and go to copilot.microsoft.com, or open the Microsoft Copilot app on your phone or computer. A chat screen appears with a text box near the bottom — usually labeled something like "Ask me anything" or "Message Copilot." If you're not signed in, sign in with your Microsoft account. You may see a few suggested prompts above the text box (like "Plan a trip" or "Write a poem"); ignore them for now.

💬 If your screen looks different — for example, you see a Copilot sidebar inside Word or Outlook — that's Microsoft 365 Copilot, which needs a paid plan. For a simple FAQ draft, the free web version is enough and works the same way.

You'll know it worked when you see a blank chat box waiting for your first message, with a send arrow on the right side.

## Step 3 — Tell Copilot about your business and draft your first answer
Click into the chat box and type a short description of your business, your customer, and the tone you want, then paste your first question and ask Copilot to write a clear answer. Two or three sentences of context is plenty: what you sell, who buys it, and whether you want the tone warm, brief, or professional. The clearer your setup, the closer the first draft comes to what you'd actually publish.

💬 Example: "I'm a small online bookstore that sells used fiction to readers in the US and Canada. Tone: friendly, brief, no jargon. My first FAQ question: 'Do you ship internationally?' Write a 2–3 sentence answer — be honest that we currently ship only to US and Canada, mention the typical delivery time, and offer an email for questions."

You'll know it worked when Copilot returns a short, plain-English answer that sounds like something you'd actually say to a customer — not generic marketing copy and not a corporate apology.

## Step 4 — Generate the rest of your FAQ in one go
Stay in the same chat and feed Copilot your remaining questions in a single message. Be specific about the format you want — numbered list, Q: / A: pairs, or a simple table — so the output is easy to copy into a document later. Ask it to keep each answer short (2–4 sentences) and to flag at the end any question where it needs more information from you. Don't expect perfection here; this is a first draft, not a finished document.

💬 Example: "Now write answers for these questions, in the same friendly tone. Format each as: Q: [question] / A: [answer], with a blank line between pairs. Keep answers 2–4 sentences. Questions: 1. How long does shipping take? 2. Can I return a book if I don't like it? 3. Do you offer gift wrapping? 4. How do I track my order? 5. Do you buy used books from customers? At the end, list any questions where you need more info from me."

You'll know it worked when you can copy a clean block of Q&A pairs with one click, and Copilot tells you which answers it had to guess at.

## Step 5 — Polish the draft into your final FAQ
Copy Copilot's output into a Google Doc, a Word file, or the Notes app on your phone. Read every answer out loud — yes, out loud — and fix anything that sounds stiff, vague, or just wrong. Cut filler phrases like "absolutely" or "great question." Add the specific facts only you know: exact shipping times in days, the real return window, your actual prices. If one answer is missing, type a follow-up in the same chat, like: "Rewrite the answer to Q2 using this policy: customers can return any book within 30 days for a full refund, sale items are final."

💬 Example follow-up prompt: "For Q3 'Do you offer gift wrapping?' — yes, $4 per book, free over $50. Rewrite the answer to match."

You'll know it worked when you have a clean, short FAQ that reads like you wrote it on a good day, not like a robot wrote it on any day.

## Step 6 — Save the FAQ and decide where it lives
Save the finished FAQ as a single document — a Google Doc, a Word file, or a new page in your website builder. From here you have two easy uses: paste it as a "FAQ" page on your website, or copy individual answers into email and chat auto-replies whenever the same question shows up again. Tell at least one teammate where the file lives. Copilot can't post anything to your website or send replies on your behalf, so this final mile is on you — but the writing part is finished.

You'll know it worked when you have a saved FAQ file you can open from any device, and your team knows exactly where to find it the next time someone asks the same question twice.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting customer names, emails, or order numbers into Copilot.** Strip out anything personal before you copy a real support thread into the chat. The free version may use your input to improve its models, and your customers' details don't belong in that pipeline.
- **Publishing the first draft without reading it.** Copilot drafts — you decide. It can write a confident, polite answer that is simply wrong about your return policy or your shipping zones. Read every line before it goes live.
- **Trying to make the FAQ perfect in one prompt.** It won't be. Plan one or two short follow-up messages per answer that needs tightening. Polish is a feature, not a step you can skip.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same technique works for any repetitive writing — a "frequently asked" note for your kid's school group chat, a family group email about holiday plans, or a standard reply for relatives who ask the same question every week.
- **For your business or work:** a finished FAQ cuts down on repeat questions, gives new hires a quick reference, and quietly improves your customer service without hiring anyone. You can also reuse the same Q&A pairs as email templates or chatbot replies.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is to draft three answers tonight and post them on your website this week. Three is enough to help — you don't need fifty.

## Try it now
Open copilot.microsoft.com, paste one real customer question into the chat, and ask Copilot for a 2–3 sentence friendly answer. Read it out loud, tweak one phrase so it sounds like you, and save it in a note. That's your first FAQ entry — the rest is just more of the same.
